Lockheed Martin vs. General Dynamics: Which Dividend Stock Pays You More in 10 Years?
sum: - Lockheed Martin (LMT) raised its quarterly dividend to $3.60 a share on Oct. 9, and General Dynamics (GD) raised its 2026 earnings forecast again on Oct. 30.
- Both companies grew their dividends 6.4% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025, but Lockheed yields 2.4% against General Dynamics’s 1.7%.
- General Dynamics pays out 29% of its free cash flow over the trailing 12 months, against Lockheed’s 38%, so its dividend has more room.
- Lockheed’s 10-year F-35 framework with the Pentagon still needs approval and funding from Congress, and Lockheed is putting up at least $7 billion of its own money to support it.
Lockheed Martin raised its quarterly dividend to $3.60 a share on Oct. 9, up from $3.45. On its Q3 call, it called the raise “our 24th consecutive year of dividend increases.”

Eight days after that call, General Dynamics raised its full-year 2026 earnings forecast again, to $17.20-$17.30 a share. Over the five years to fiscal 2025, the two grew their dividends at exactly the same pace: 6.4% a year.
So if both keep that pace, which one pays you more over the next 10 years?

General Dynamics stock gains as record backlog supports growth outlook
sum: General Dynamics stock traded at 332.00 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 13:44 CET on Thursday, November 12, 2026, 1.03% above the Xetra close of Wednesday, November 11, at 328.60 euros. The comparison follows the strong third-quarter performance and record order intake reported by General Dynamics on October 30.

In its third-quarter financial release, the company said revenue rose 12.9% year over year to 14.566 billion US dollars for the period ended October 4, 2026. Operating earnings increased 14.7% to 1.527 billion US dollars, while diluted earnings per share advanced 15.7% to 4.49 US dollars.

Order intake was the main structural feature of the quarter. General Dynamics received 98.8 billion US dollars of orders, including 93.8 billion US dollars in its defense segments and 5 billion US dollars in Aerospace. The company-wide book-to-bill ratio reached 6.8 to 1, indicating that new orders substantially exceeded quarterly revenue.

Backlog stood at 220.3 billion US dollars at the quarter end, compared with 136.5 billion US dollars in the second quarter and 109.9 billion US dollars a year earlier. Marine Systems accounted for 146.9 billion US dollars of the total, with major Virginia-class and Columbia-class submarine awards driving the sharp increase.

The backlog provides long-term visibility, but it also raises execution requirements. Shipyard capacity, workforce expansion and delivery schedules will determine how quickly the awards translate into revenue and cash flow. General Dynamics generated 1.7 billion US dollars of operating cash flow in the quarter and invested 481 million US dollars in capital expenditures.

Marine Systems revenue increased 21.1% year over year to 4.960 billion US dollars, the strongest growth among the company's four businesses. Aerospace revenue rose 9.3% to 3.536 billion US dollars, Combat Systems grew 6.0% to 2.386 billion US dollars and Technologies advanced 10.8% to 3.684 billion US dollars.

Aerospace also expanded operating earnings by 19.3% to 513 million US dollars, while Marine Systems increased operating earnings by 34.4% to 391 million US dollars. Combat Systems earnings slipped 1.5%, showing that the order surge does not remove the need for consistent program execution across the portfolio.

sum: General Dynamics raised its 2026 earnings outlook again after strong third-quarter execution, lifting the financial bar for its defense, shipbuilding and business-jet operations. Zacks Equity Research reported the updated targets on Monday, November 2, citing management's earnings-call comments.
General Dynamics stock traded at 329.85 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 14:04 CET on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

Chief executive Phebe Novakovic raised the full-year diluted earnings outlook to 17.20 to 17.30 US dollars per share from 16.80 to 16.90 US dollars. Management also set revenue guidance at 56.5 billion to 56.8 billion US dollars and kept operating-margin guidance near 10.5 percent.

The increase followed third-quarter earnings of 4.49 US dollars per diluted share, ahead of the 4.14 US dollar consensus cited by Zacks. Quarterly revenue reached 14.57 billion US dollars, compared with a consensus estimate of 13.69 billion US dollars.

The company has now raised its full-year earnings outlook three times in 2026, according to the report. Management plans to provide its 2027 outlook in January after completing the annual planning process.

Quarterly orders of nearly 99 billion US dollars lifted consolidated backlog to a record 220.3 billion US dollars. Marine Systems accounted for 146.9 billion US dollars, supported by 29.5 billion US dollars of awards for five additional Columbia-class submarines and 42.1 billion US dollars for nine additional Virginia-class submarines.

The backlog gives General Dynamics considerable revenue visibility, but it also raises the importance of delivery discipline. Zacks reported that management sees shipyard productivity as a central margin lever. A favorable one-time cumulative adjustment helped Marine Systems reach a 7.9 percent margin in the quarter; excluding that effect, management described the mid-7 percent range as the baseline, with further improvement dependent on productivity.

Lockheed Martin Stock: Record $292 Billion Backlog, $8 Billion Missile Bet, and a Price Worth Watching
sum: Lockheed Martin has had a quiet but successful run. Among the leading American aerospace and defense companies, the stock outperformed RTX, General Dynamics, Northrop Grumman, and L3Harris with a 25.1% return over the previous year. However, Lockheed trades at a lower earnings multiple than the majority of those same peers when you consider how the market is pricing it. Analysts and investors are currently reexamining LMT due to this tension—strong performance, relatively modest valuation.

The stock is currently trading between $567 and $570 per share, down from a 52-week high of $692 reached in March 2026. There has been a real pullback, with some of it occurring rapidly. Following the midterm election results that gave Democrats control of both the Senate and the House, the stock fell nearly 7% in a single session on November 4, prompting immediate worries about the size of future defense budgets. That response makes sense because the defense sector is closely linked to federal spending decisions, but considering Lockheed’s current order book’s structural makeup, it might also be a little hasty.

That order book is exceptional. The company had a record backlog of $292 billion at the end of the third quarter of 2026, up $113 billion from just a year earlier. The largest contribution in the third quarter came from a single seven-year PAC-3 interceptor contract, which had a total value of up to $58.6 billion. A $35 billion, seven-year THAAD agreement was also signed earlier this year. These pipeline items are not speculative. Lockheed has a level of revenue visibility that most industrial companies would be jealous of thanks to these signed, long-term commitments.

The momentum was strengthened by the third-quarter results, which were released on October 22. Revenue increased by 11.3% year over year to almost $21 billion. Each business sector expanded. Missiles and Fire Control stood out, reporting a 24% increase, which was fueled by precisely the kinds of initiatives those large contracts are supporting. The management increased the sales forecast for the entire year 2026 to a midpoint of $81 billion, suggesting a growth of about 8%. They anticipate that all four segments will contribute to high single-digit growth in 2027.

US Defense Stocks Plunge as Democrats Poised for Midterm Landslide; Doubts Mount Over $1.5 Trillion Defense Budget
sum: Defense stocks fell across the board on the US stock market on Nov. 4. Following projections that Democrats will capture both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, concerns spread that Congress will tighten its grip on Pentagon spending plans and new procurement programs.

The steepest decliner was Lockheed Martin (LMT), down 6.9%. RTX (RTX), which makes missiles and radar systems, fell about 3%, and L3Harris Technologies (LHX) dropped more than 6%. General Dynamics (GD) and Northrop Grumman (NOC) also were sold off. The S&P 500 aerospace and defense sub-index is down about 1% year to date, and the Dow Jones US aerospace and defense sub-index is down 3.4%, with the day's losses pushing their year-to-date performance into negative territory.

The defense sector had until now been buoyed by President Trump's proposed $1.5 trillion (approximately ¥236.9 trillion) military budget for fiscal 2027 — a large-scale increase — and by rising demand for missiles and air defense systems tied to the Iran war. However, the prevailing view is that the Democratic-led House will impose stricter scrutiny on the defense budget and new programs.

Jefferies analysts wrote in a report that they expect the fiscal 2027 defense budget to settle at a level closer to the roughly $1.15 trillion (approximately ¥181.6 trillion) proposed by the House, rather than the $1.5 trillion sought by the administration. Roman Schweizer, an analyst at TD Cowen, said "Trump's 'signature' programs are dead," indicating that the nationwide missile defense initiative "Golden Dome" and the "Golden Fleet" modernization plan centered on new "Trump-class" battleships will take a hit.

On the other hand, according to Schweizer, programs related to nuclear force modernization — such as the B21 bomber manufactured by Northrop and the new intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) "Sentinel" — carry the lowest risk. Analysts broadly share the view that support for military modernization itself will largely be maintained, which is keeping full-blown pessimism in check.
Note: Declines are intraday figures. GD and NOC are listed as "under selling pressure" because specific decline percentages were not disclosed.

items.t: U.S. stocks surge, and the Dow soars 1,500 points as oil prices tumble following the U.S. midterm elections
sum: NEW YORK — U.S. stocks soared Wednesday after U.S. President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.

Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6 per cent for its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569 points, or 3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.4 per cent.

Stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally following the nationwide losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil also tumbled below US$95 and touched its lowest level in two months. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans’ midterm losses on the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices.

Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington.
“Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.

Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.

General Dynamics upgraded to Buy as submarine boom fuels growth outlook
sum: Investing.com -- General Dynamics received a rating upgrade from Jefferies, which raised its recommendation to Buy from Hold and increased its price target to $400 from $380, arguing that accelerating demand for U.S. Navy submarines and improving shipyard productivity position the defense contractor for stronger earnings growth in the years ahead.

Jefferies said General Dynamics' Marine Systems business, which accounts for roughly a third of company revenue, continues to outperform expectations, with first-quarter sales rising 21% year-over-year versus the company's full-year guidance for 3% to 6% growth. The brokerage sees upside from a growing submarine backlog, improving labor productivity and margin expansion as production ramps on Virginia-class and Columbia-class submarine programs.

The bullish view is underpinned by the U.S. Navy's latest shipbuilding plan, which includes $125 billion of submarine procurement funding between fiscal 2027 and 2031, alongside billions of dollars earmarked for shipyard modernization, workforce development and productivity improvements. Jefferies said these investments support a path toward producing one Columbia-class and two Virginia-class submarines annually.

General Dynamics has already invested more than $4 billion in its Electric Boat shipyard over the past decade and plans to spend another $4 billion over the next five years while expanding its workforce. The company expects to hire more than 8,000 employees in 2026 to support rising submarine production.

Jefferies forecasts Marine Systems revenue will grow at a 6% compound annual rate through 2028, driven primarily by nuclear submarines, while operating margins improve from 7.0% in 2025 to 7.5% in 2026 and 7.8% by 2028 as productivity gains take hold.

The brokerage also cited continued strength in Gulfstream business jet deliveries and the potential for shareholder returns, estimating the company could generate about $3 billion of discretionary free cash flow after dividends in 2027. Shares closed at $341.07 prior to the report, implying roughly 17% upside to Jefferies' new target price.

items.t: General Dynamics stock heads toward October 28 earnings with backlog strength
sum: General Dynamics stock (ISIN US3695501086) was trading at USD 332.53 on the NYSE on October 6, 2026, at 11:42 a.m. ET, up 0.24 percent from the prior close. The next earnings report is scheduled for October 28, 2026, according to Investing.com.

The date matters because General Dynamics enters the report with a sizable operating base. In the second quarter ended July 5, 2026, revenue reached USD 14.1 billion, up 8.1 percent from the year-earlier quarter, while diluted EPS rose 13.4 percent to USD 4.24, according to Yahoo Finance.

The same transcript shows operating margin at 10.4 percent, an improvement of 40 basis points from the year-earlier quarter. That combination of higher sales and wider margin gives the October report two measurable checkpoints: execution against demand and the pace of cost improvement.

General Dynamics ended Q2 with a record backlog of USD 136.5 billion, up 32 percent year over year, according to Yahoo Finance. The company also reported a 1.4 to 1 book-to-bill ratio for the quarter, indicating that orders exceeded recognized revenue across the business.

Management raised full-year 2026 diluted EPS guidance to USD 16.80-16.90 from USD 16.45-16.55, the transcript said. The key investor question is whether aerospace deliveries, shipyard productivity and defense demand can convert that backlog into sustained margin expansion.

Consensus remains Buy, with 16 analysts covering General Dynamics and an average 12-month price target of USD 423.39, according to Rallies. The average target lies 27.3 percent above the USD 332.53 price, making the October earnings release the next concrete test of that valuation view.

General Dynamics shares surge after raising 2026 profit guidance
sum: April 29 (Reuters) - General Dynamics on Wednesday lifted its annual profit forecast and beat Wall Street estimates for first-quarter profit and revenue, driven by continued strength in its marine and aerospace segments.
Shares of the Reston, Virginia-based company rose over 10% in early trading in New York, setting them on track for their best one-day jump since October 2008.

Robust defense demand amid ongoing global conflicts continued to drive higher sales across all segments during the quarter, while the company recovers from supply chain disruptions and ramps up production. The Pentagon unveiled a $1.5 trillion defense budget request for fiscal year 2027 earlier this month, including $65 billion for shipbuilding.
General Dynamics now expects full-year 2026 profit between $16.45 and $16.55 per share, compared with its previous projection of $16.10 to $16.20 per share.
Quarterly revenue in the marine systems segment rose 21% from a year ago, driven by higher production volumes on the Virginia‑ and Columbia‑class submarine programs.
General Dynamics reported strong order activity, with quarterly bookings running at roughly twice the level of billings, boosting the overall backlog.
In the aerospace segment, which makes Gulfstream business jets, revenue rose 8.4% as manufacturing volumes improved and services business strength held up.

General Dynamics gets unexpected War Department win ahead of earnings
sum: Eight months ago, the U.S. Army quietly told General Dynamics (GD) to stop work on a $591 million artillery shell factory in Texas. No public explanation. No timeline for resolution. Just a work stoppage order on a plant that had already opened, and still hadn't produced a single shell.
For a defense contractor heading into earnings week, that's not the kind of story you want hanging over the stock.

But something interesting has happened. And it is big. The Army lifted that stoppage order, Bloomberg reported Monday, and is now working with the 133-year-old Virginia-based General Dynamics (GD) on "the way forward" for the facility, a plant designed to produce 30,000 155mm artillery shells per month across three production lines.

The timing here is also very interesting and striking. General Dynamics reports first-quarter 2026 earnings on April 29, and the ammunition plant's revival gives CEO Phebe Novakovic something constructive to say about a program that had become a visible execution question mark, in the middle of a war that is consuming 155mm shells at a significant rate.
"As we focus on execution of programs for our customers, we are also preparing aggressively for future growth," Novakovic said in the company's most recent earnings commentary.
Here's why General Dynamics' Texas ammunition plant revival matters now

The backstory on the Texas facility makes the Army's reversal more significant than a routine contract update. The plant opened in May 2024 and was contractually obligated to reach production of 30,000 155mm artillery shells per month. It never did.

items.t: GE Aerospace Rallies 51.5% in a Year: Is the Stock Still Worth Buying?
sum: GE Aerospace's GE investors have been witnessing impressive gains from the stock of late. Shares of the leading designer and producer of jet engines have surged 51.5% in the past year, outpacing the S&P 500 composite and industry's growth of 16.9% and 28.2%, respectively. The company has also outperformed other industry players like General Dynamics Corporation GD and Textron Inc. TXT, which have returned 39.6% and 29.6%, respectively, over the said time frame.

Closing at $316.33 on Tuesday, the stock is trading close to its 52-week high of $332.79 but significantly higher than its 52-week low of $159.36. Also, the stock is trading above both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages, indicating solid upward momentum and price stability. This reflects a positive market sentiment and confidence in the company's financial health and long-term prospects.

GE Aerospace is benefiting from a growing installed base and higher utilization of engine platforms, driven by strong momentum and growth across commercial & defense sectors. Solid demand for LEAP, GEnx & GE9X engines and services, supported by growth in air traffic, fleet renewal and expansion activities, is proving beneficial for the Commercial Engines & Services business. During 2025, the company secured more than 500 engine wins at the Dubai Airshow, including deals from flydubai for GEnx engines and Riyadh Air for LEAP-1A engines.

It also inked a deal with Qatar Airways to supply more than 400 GE9X and GEnx engines. It represents the largest widebody engine deal in GE Aerospace's history. The Commercial Engines & Services business' revenues and orders jumped 24% and 35%, respectively, on a year-over-year basis in 2025.

Growing popularity for the company's propulsion & additive technologies, critical aircraft systems and aftermarket services in the defense sector is driving GE's Defense & Propulsion Technologies business' performance. During 2025, the company secured a $5 billion contract from the U.S. Air Force to supply F110 engines, parts and support services as part of a Foreign Military Sales (FMS) program. Also, GE received an Indefinite Delivery Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) contract from the U.S. Army to supply F110 engines for F-15 and F-16 jets.

items.t: Trump says he will not permit dividends and stock buybacks for defense companies
sum: President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he "will not permit" defense companies to issue dividends or stock buybacks until those firms speed up their production of military equipment and address his other complaints about the industry.
Trump, in a lengthy Truth Social post, also took aim at defense contractors' executive pay packages, calling them "exorbitant and unjustifiable."
"Defense Companies are not producing our Great Military Equipment rapidly enough and, once produced, not maintaining it properly or quickly," he wrote.
Until those companies build new production plants, "no Executive should be allowed to make in excess of $5 Million Dollars," Trump declared.
Shares of General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman each fell about 3% following Trump's comments.

Trump later singled out Raytheon as "the least responsive to the needs of the Department of War, the slowest in increasing their volume, and the most aggressive spending on their Shareholders rather than the needs and demands of the United States Military."

He said that the Pentagon will cut its business ties with Raytheon unless it "steps up" on investment in plants and equipment, adding that "under no circumstances" can the company do any more stock buybacks in the meantime.

sum: Today we're going to take a look at the well-established Cintas Corporation (NASDAQ:CTAS). The company's stock saw significant share price movement during recent months on the NASDAQGS, rising to highs of US$205 and falling to the lows of US$182. Some share price movements can give investors a better opportunity to enter into the stock, and potentially buy at a lower price. A question to answer is whether Cintas' current trading price of US$185 reflective of the actual value of the large-cap? Or is it currently undervalued, providing us with the opportunity to buy? Let’s take a look at Cintas’s outlook and value based on the most recent financial data to see if there are any catalysts for a price change.

The stock seems fairly valued at the moment according to our valuation model. It’s trading around 14.47% above our intrinsic value, which means if you buy Cintas today, you’d be paying a relatively reasonable price for it. And if you believe that the stock is really worth $162.02, then there isn’t really any room for the share price grow beyond what it’s currently trading. What's more, Cintas’s share price may be more stable over time (relative to the market), as indicated by its low beta.

Investors looking for growth in their portfolio may want to consider the prospects of a company before buying its shares. Although value investors would argue that it’s the intrinsic value relative to the price that matter the most, a more compelling investment thesis would be high growth potential at a cheap price. With profit expected to grow by 32% over the next couple of years, the future seems bright for Cintas. It looks like higher cash flow is on the cards for the stock, which should feed into a higher share valuation.

Are you a shareholder? CTAS’s optimistic future growth appears to have been factored into the current share price, with shares trading around its fair value. However, there are also other important factors which we haven’t considered today, such as the track record of its management team. Have these factors changed since the last time you looked at the stock? Will you have enough confidence to invest in the company should the price drop below its fair value?
